questions.stem: The slogan 'populate or perish', associated with Arthur Calwell as the first Minister for Immigration, expressed the belief that Australia needed:
options: a smaller population so that wages and housing would be protected
to replace British migrants with workers recruited from Asia
to encourage returned servicemen to settle back in Britain
a much larger population for its defence and economic development
questions.explanation: The Pacific War convinced many that a small population could not defend the continent or develop its industries, so the government set out to increase immigration sharply. The program still drew overwhelmingly on Britain and Europe, not Asia.

questions.stem: Under the Assisted Passage Scheme introduced after the Second World War, many British migrants:
options: travelled to Australia for a fare of only ten pounds
received free farmland in return for military service
had to work for two years wherever the government directed
were required to pass a dictation test in English on arrival
questions.explanation: Adult British migrants paid ten pounds towards their passage, earning the nickname 'Ten Pound Poms'. The two-year work obligation applied to displaced persons, not to assisted British migrants.

questions.stem: Displaced persons from Europe who came to Australia under the scheme agreed with the International Refugee Organization in 1947 had to:
options: become Australian citizens before they were allowed to land
settle only in capital cities close to a migrant hostel
repay the full cost of their sea passage within their first year
work for two years in jobs and places chosen by the government
questions.explanation: In return for resettlement, displaced persons signed contracts to work for two years wherever they were sent, often on construction projects, in factories or in rural areas. This supplied labour for post-war development while limiting migrants' choices.

questions.stem: Bonegilla, near Wodonga in Victoria, is significant in post-war migration history as:
options: a Snowy Mountains construction town built for British engineers
a Melbourne suburb where the first Greek community settled
a migrant reception and training centre where many arrivals first lived
a detention centre for the asylum seekers who arrived by boat in the 1970s
questions.explanation: Bonegilla operated from 1947 to 1971 and housed hundreds of thousands of new arrivals, mostly from continental Europe, while they were processed, given English lessons and allocated work. It closed before the Indochinese refugee arrivals.

questions.stem: Calwell chose many of the first displaced persons from the Baltic states. Historians generally explain this choice as an attempt to:
options: recruit farmers, because the Baltic states had been the main suppliers of wheat
win public acceptance with migrants he expected Australians to see as similar to themselves
attract migrants who already spoke fluent English and had British qualifications
fulfil a treaty under which Australia had to accept refugees from Soviet territory
questions.explanation: Calwell knew many Australians were wary of non-British migrants, and he publicised young, fair-haired Baltic arrivals to build support for the wider program. Most did not speak English on arrival.

questions.stem: In 1949 the High Court ruled that Annie O'Keefe, an Indonesian woman who had come to Australia as a wartime refugee, could not be deported. Calwell's response shows the continuing force of White Australia because he:
options: abolished the dictation test so that future cases could be decided by the courts
granted permanent residence to all wartime refugees, whatever their background
appealed to the Privy Council, which reversed the decision of the High Court
passed a new law, the Wartime Refugees Removal Act, to allow such deportations
questions.explanation: After losing the case, the government passed the Wartime Refugees Removal Act 1949 to deport non-European wartime refugees. The episode shows a government determined to keep the policy despite a court ruling and criticism from Asian neighbours.

questions.stem: In the early 1950s Australia signed assisted migration agreements with countries such as Italy and Greece. These agreements showed the government:
options: deciding to stop assisted British migration because too few British applied
widening its intake beyond Britain for labour while still excluding non-Europeans
ending the White Australia policy in favour of selection by skills and family ties
agreeing to resettle refugees from Asia under the supervision of the United Nations
questions.explanation: Labour shortages pushed governments to recruit from southern Europe, which changed the make-up of the population. Non-European migration remained restricted until the policy was dismantled from the late 1950s to 1973.

questions.stem: The Nationality and Citizenship Act 1948:
options: created Australian citizenship, which began on 26 January 1949
abolished the dictation test and replaced it with entry permits
gave all Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections
ended the assisted passage scheme for migrants from Britain
questions.explanation: Before 1949 Australians were British subjects; the Act created a distinct Australian citizenship while keeping British subject status. The dictation test was abolished separately by the Migration Act 1958.

questions.stem: Under the assimilation policy of the 1950s, newly arrived migrants were expected to:
options: learn English, adopt Australian ways and blend into the community
keep their own languages through government-funded community schools
live in separate districts so that their cultures could be preserved
return to their homelands once their two-year work contracts ended
questions.explanation: Assimilation assumed that migrants would quickly become indistinguishable from other Australians, and government programs such as 'New Australian' publicity reflected this. Funding for community languages came later, under multiculturalism.

questions.stem: In 1961 Commonwealth and state ministers agreed a definition of the assimilation policy for Aboriginal people. It said that Aboriginal people were expected to:
options: attain the same manner of living as other Australians in a single community
govern their own communities on reserves according to their own customary laws
receive land rights over their traditional Country in each state
be recognised as distinct nations with whom treaties would be made
questions.explanation: The 1961 statement expected Aboriginal people to live like other Australians, sharing the same customs, beliefs and loyalties. It assumed Aboriginal cultures would disappear, and it was later criticised for justifying child removal and the loss of identity.

questions.stem: Australia's H. V. Evatt was President of the United Nations General Assembly when it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. The Declaration became significant in Australian debates because it:
options: was written into the Australian Constitution by referendum in the 1950s
asserted equal rights regardless of race, exposing contradictions in Australian policy
required Australia to admit refugees from every country whose citizens applied to resettle
ordered Australia to repeal the Immigration Restriction Act within ten years
questions.explanation: The Declaration set out rights belonging to everyone without distinction of race, and critics used it to challenge racial immigration laws and discrimination against Aboriginal people. It was not legally binding and did not change the Constitution.

questions.stem: Decolonisation in Asia after 1945, as countries such as India and Indonesia gained independence, put pressure on the White Australia policy mainly because:
options: Britain required Australia to accept migrants from all of its former colonies
Asian independence leaders urged Australia to remain a British colony
newly independent Asian nations criticised it, damaging Australia's regional relations
Asian nations demanded that Australia leave the Commonwealth of Nations and its institutions
questions.explanation: Australia wanted friendly relations and trade with its new neighbours, but its racially based immigration policy was widely seen in Asia as insulting. This regional pressure helped persuade governments to soften and then end the policy.

questions.stem: The Colombo Plan, begun in 1950, contributed to changing attitudes in Australia because it:
options: committed Australia to defend Asian nations against invasion
brought many students from Asia to study at Australian institutions
allowed workers from Asia to settle permanently on Australian farms
resettled displaced persons from Europe in rural Australian towns
questions.explanation: Through the Colombo Plan, thousands of Asian students studied in Australia, increasing everyday contact and goodwill. Students were expected to return home, so it did not itself open permanent migration.

questions.stem: The Immigration Reform Group's 1960 pamphlet 'Immigration: Control or Colour Bar?':
options: called for an end to all immigration until unemployment had been reduced
proposed replacing the dictation test with a test in Asian languages
criticised White Australia and proposed a small, non-racial intake from Asia
defended White Australia as essential to social cohesion and full employment
questions.explanation: The Melbourne-based group argued that racial exclusion was unjust and damaging to Australia's standing, and suggested a controlled intake selected without regard to race. It was an influential critique of the policy from within Australia.

questions.stem: The Migration Act 1958:
options: ended the White Australia policy and removed race from all selection
made racial discrimination unlawful in employment and housing
created Australian citizenship separate from British subject status
abolished the dictation test and introduced a system of entry permits
questions.explanation: The Act removed the notorious dictation test and gave the minister power to grant entry permits, but selection still favoured Europeans. Race was not formally removed from selection until 1973.

questions.stem: In 1966 the Holt government changed migration policy so that:
options: well-qualified non-Europeans could apply, and could become citizens after five years
all migrants were selected by a points test, without any regard to their race or origin
multiculturalism became the official policy of the Commonwealth government
refugees fleeing the Vietnam War were accepted as permanent residents
questions.explanation: The 1966 reforms let non-Europeans with useful qualifications apply to settle and cut their wait for citizenship from fifteen to five years, the same as for Europeans. It was a major step, but race was not formally removed from selection until 1973.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum changed the Constitution by:
options: including Aboriginal people in the race power and deleting section 127
giving all Aboriginal people the right to vote in Commonwealth elections
granting Aboriginal people Australian citizenship for the first time
creating land rights for Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory
questions.explanation: The referendum removed the words excluding 'the aboriginal race in any State' from section 51(xxvi), letting the Commonwealth make laws for Aboriginal people, and deleted section 127 so they would be counted in the population. It did not deal with voting or citizenship.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The 1967 referendum gave Aboriginal people the vote.' Which is the most accurate correction?
options: Aboriginal people first gained the vote only when enrolment became compulsory
The referendum gave the vote only to Aboriginal people who had served in war
The referendum gave the vote in federal elections but not citizenship
All Aboriginal people could already enrol for federal elections from 1962
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Electoral Act 1962 gave all Aboriginal people the right to enrol and vote in federal elections, five years before the referendum. Compulsory enrolment for Aboriginal people came later, in 1984, but the right to vote already existed.

questions.stem: The 1967 referendum was carried with over 90 per cent of the national vote and a majority in all six states. Historians treat it as significant mainly because it:
options: immediately ended discriminatory laws in every state, including the remaining protection Acts
recognised native title, so Aboriginal land claims could be heard by the High Court
ended the assimilation policy and replaced it with self-determination the same year
let the Commonwealth make laws for Aboriginal people and showed broad public support for change
questions.explanation: The vote was an extraordinary show of public goodwill and gave the Commonwealth a power it later used for Aboriginal affairs. Change was slow, however: discriminatory state laws were not swept away overnight, and self-determination became policy only in the 1970s.

questions.stem: In 1973 the Whitlam government's Minister for Immigration, who became closely associated with the idea of a multicultural society, was:
options: Arthur Calwell
Harold Holt
Malcolm Fraser
Al Grassby
questions.explanation: Al Grassby promoted the term 'multicultural' in a 1973 speech about Australia's future. Calwell had been the first Minister for Immigration in the 1940s, and Holt's government made the 1966 reforms.

questions.stem: The Whitlam government's 1973 immigration policy is often described as the formal end of the White Australia policy because it:
options: created Australian citizenship for migrants
admitted refugees arriving by boat from Vietnam
removed race as a factor in selecting migrants
abolished the dictation test for the first time
questions.explanation: From 1973 the government declared that migrants would be selected without regard to race, colour or nationality. The dictation test had already gone in 1958, and the first refugee boats from Vietnam arrived in 1976.

questions.stem: For migrant communities, the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 made it unlawful to:
options: teach community languages in government schools without formal approval from the Commonwealth
settle in a city other than the one named in an assisted migrant's travel documents
publish newspapers in languages other than English without a translation for officials
discriminate against people on the basis of race, colour, descent or national or ethnic origin
questions.explanation: The Act gave effect to an international convention against racial discrimination and covered areas such as employment, housing and access to services. It was a legal foundation for a multicultural society, not a restriction on migrant cultures.

questions.stem: The fall of Saigon in 1975 led to:
options: the arrival of Vietnamese refugees, including boat arrivals from 1976
the end of national service conscription in Australia that year
Australia's first commitment of combat troops to the war in Vietnam
the closure of the Bonegilla migrant centre the following year
questions.explanation: After the communist victory, many Vietnamese fled, and the first boat carrying refugees reached Darwin in 1976. Conscription had ended in 1972 and Bonegilla closed in 1971.

questions.stem: The Fraser government's response to refugees from Indochina in the late 1970s was to:
options: send all refugees to offshore processing centres on Nauru
accept refugees only if they already had relatives in Australia
resettle large numbers, most selected from camps in South-East Asia
refuse to resettle anyone at all who had travelled to Australia by boat
questions.explanation: Fraser's government resettled tens of thousands of Indochinese refugees, mostly through orderly selection from camps in the region, while accepting those who arrived by boat. Offshore processing on Nauru belongs to 2001, not the 1970s.

questions.stem: The Galbally Report of 1978, commissioned by the Fraser government:
options: recommended reducing family reunion and returning to the earlier policy of assimilation
recommended the mandatory detention of all people arriving without a visa
recommended ending assisted passages and closing all migrant hostels at once
recommended services for migrants and multicultural programs, including television
questions.explanation: The report led to funding for migrant resource centres, English classes and ethnic community services, and supported multicultural broadcasting, which became SBS television in 1980. It entrenched multiculturalism as bipartisan policy for a time.

questions.stem: A government funds community-language radio, translates its services and supports ethnic community organisations, while expecting commitment to Australia's laws and institutions. This policy best reflects:
options: assimilation, as practised in the 1950s and early 1960s
the White Australia policy in its final years
the 'populate or perish' program of the late 1940s
multiculturalism, as developed in the 1970s and 1980s
questions.explanation: Multicultural policy accepted that migrants could keep their languages and cultures, with government support, within shared civic values. Assimilation expected migrants to abandon their cultures and blend in.

questions.stem: In 1984 the historian Geoffrey Blainey caused national controversy when he argued that:
options: Asian immigration should be increased quickly to strengthen trade with the region
the rate of Asian immigration was moving faster than public opinion would accept
Australia should end all immigration from Europe in favour of migrants from Asia
the Commonwealth should apologise to the Stolen Generations and pay compensation
questions.explanation: Speaking at Warrnambool and later in his book 'All for Australia', Blainey said the level of Asian immigration was outrunning community acceptance. Supporters saw a call for caution; critics saw a revival of racial thinking.

questions.stem: The 1984 Blainey controversy is significant in the history of immigration debates mainly because it showed that:
options: the Hawke government was willing to abandon multicultural policies when they were criticised
public pressure could force the government to bring back the dictation test
Australia would now set a fixed quota on the number of migrants from Asia
arguments about the pace and source of immigration continued after White Australia ended
questions.explanation: The government did not change its non-discriminatory policy, but the debate revealed continuing anxiety about Asian immigration. It is an example of continuity in debates about race and belonging after the formal end of White Australia.

questions.stem: After the Tiananmen Square massacre of June 1989, Prime Minister Bob Hawke:
options: closed the Chinese embassy in Canberra and expelled its diplomats
ended all trade with China until the government there had changed
deported the Chinese students who had protested in Australian cities
announced that Chinese students in Australia would be allowed to stay
questions.explanation: Hawke announced that Chinese students would not be forced to return, and many later received permanent residence. The decision was humanitarian but also controversial, because it bypassed the usual migration rules.

questions.stem: In 1992 the Keating government introduced a policy that has shaped border security debates ever since. It was:
options: the formal end of the White Australia policy and the dictation test
the creation of a points test for selecting skilled migrants
the first resettlement program for refugees from Indochina
the mandatory detention of people who arrived by boat without a visa
questions.explanation: Mandatory detention was introduced in 1992, mainly in response to boat arrivals from Cambodia, and it was later maintained by governments of both major parties. The White Australia policy and the dictation test had ended decades earlier.

questions.stem: In her maiden speech to parliament in 1996, Pauline Hanson:
options: argued for a large increase in Australia's refugee intake
urged closer economic and political integration with Asia
warned that Australia was in danger of being 'swamped by Asians'
called for a treaty with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
questions.explanation: Hanson attacked multiculturalism, Asian immigration and government assistance to Aboriginal people. Her speech drew strong support from some Australians and widespread condemnation from others.

questions.stem: Historians usually link the rise of Pauline Hanson's One Nation party in the late 1990s, especially in regional areas, to:
options: a campaign against Australian involvement in the Vietnam War
demands that Australia become a republic and leave the Commonwealth
economic insecurity combined with resentment of Asian immigration and Aboriginal programs
growing support among farmers for multiculturalism and for higher immigration levels overall
questions.explanation: One Nation drew on rural and working-class anxieties about economic change, job losses and globalisation, which it connected to immigration and assistance for Aboriginal people. Its rise showed that racial politics remained potent long after 1973.

questions.stem: After the Tampa affair of 2001, the Howard government's 'Pacific Solution' meant that:
options: asylum seekers intercepted at sea were taken to Nauru and Papua New Guinea for processing
asylum seekers who reached Australia by boat were granted permanent visas on arrival
Australia withdrew from the Refugee Convention and stopped resettling any refugees
asylum seekers were processed in Darwin and released into the community within weeks
questions.explanation: The Pacific Solution sent people seeking asylum to offshore processing centres on Nauru and Manus Island, so they could not apply for protection on Australian soil. Australia remained a party to the Refugee Convention.

questions.stem: The Bringing Them Home report of 1997 was the result of:
options: a national inquiry into the separation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families
a royal commission into the deaths of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in police custody
a High Court case about the native title of the Meriam people of the Murray Islands
a ten-year review of Aboriginal reserves by the Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation
questions.explanation: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission inquiry, led by Sir Ronald Wilson and Mick Dodson, heard testimony from hundreds of people about forcible removal. The Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody was a separate inquiry that reported in 1991.

questions.stem: Among its recommendations, the Bringing Them Home report called for:
options: the closure of every remaining reserve and the transfer of residents to towns
a treaty creating a separate parliament for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
the repeal of the Racial Discrimination Act so that special measures could be taken
acknowledgement and apology by parliaments and other bodies, and reparation
questions.explanation: The report recommended that parliaments, police forces and churches acknowledge responsibility and apologise, and that reparation, including compensation, be provided. It also recommended a national 'Sorry Day', first held in 1998.

questions.stem: The Howard government declined to make a formal apology after the Bringing Them Home report. In 1999 parliament instead passed a motion that:
options: rejected the report's findings in full and closed the national inquiry
committed the government to negotiating a treaty within five years
expressed deep and sincere regret for past injustices without apologising
made a formal apology and offered compensation to every person who was removed
questions.explanation: Howard argued that the present generation should not apologise for the actions of earlier ones, and the 1999 motion of reconciliation expressed 'deep and sincere regret'. Many Aboriginal leaders saw this as falling short of the apology the report had asked for.

questions.stem: In his Redfern Park Speech of December 1992, Prime Minister Paul Keating:
options: argued that the past should be set aside so that all Australians could move forward together as one
acknowledged that non-Indigenous Australians had dispossessed Aboriginal people and taken their children
announced that the Stolen Generations would receive compensation from the Commonwealth
declared that Aboriginal people had ceded their land to the Crown through treaties
questions.explanation: Launching the International Year for the World's Indigenous People, Keating said that recognition must begin with non-Indigenous Australians admitting that 'we' took the land, brought the diseases and took the children. It was a landmark acknowledgement of dispossession by a prime minister.

questions.stem: The Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation, established in 1991 with the support of all parties, was set up to:
options: promote reconciliation between Indigenous and other Australians over ten years
hear and decide claims for compensation from members of the Stolen Generations
decide claims for native title under Commonwealth legislation
manage the remaining Aboriginal reserves on behalf of the states
questions.explanation: The Council was to work towards reconciliation by the centenary of Federation in 2001. Its work culminated in Corroboree 2000 and the walks for reconciliation, including the crossing of Sydney Harbour Bridge.

questions.stem: On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd moved a motion in parliament that:
options: committed the Commonwealth to signing a treaty with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
apologised on behalf of the Labor Party only, as the opposition refused to support it
apologised to the Stolen Generations for the laws and policies of successive governments
announced individual compensation payments for every child who had been removed
questions.explanation: The Apology said sorry for the laws and policies of successive parliaments and governments that had inflicted grief and loss, especially the removal of children. It was supported by the opposition and did not include a compensation scheme.

questions.stem: By the 1980s Cabramatta in Sydney and Victoria Street in Richmond, Melbourne, had become known as centres of which community?
options: Portuguese
Vietnamese
Italian
Greek
questions.explanation: Many refugees from Vietnam settled near migrant hostels and in areas with affordable housing, building businesses and community organisations. Italian and Greek communities had grown earlier, in suburbs such as Carlton, Brunswick and Oakleigh in Melbourne.

questions.stem: The Cronulla riots of December 2005, in which crowds attacked people of Middle Eastern appearance, are often cited by historians as evidence that:
options: migrant communities had stopped settling in Australia's large cities
racial tensions could persist in a multicultural society despite anti-discrimination laws
the Commonwealth had formally replaced multiculturalism with a policy of assimilation
the White Australia policy had been restored by legislation after 2001
questions.explanation: The riots showed that legal equality and official multiculturalism had not removed racism from everyday life. Multiculturalism remained official policy, and no racial immigration law was restored.

questions.stem: In 1989 the Hawke government helped found APEC, a forum for economic cooperation in the Asia-Pacific. This development best reflects:
options: a return to the policy of forward defence against communism in South-East Asia
Australia's decision to leave the Commonwealth and end its ties with Britain
a plan to increase migration from Britain to balance trade with Asia
a shift from seeing Asia mainly as a threat to seeing it as Australia's region
questions.explanation: In the 1850s and 1900s Asia was cast as a source of unwanted migrants and invasion; by the 1980s governments saw Asia as Australia's economic future. This change in relations helped make non-discriminatory immigration politically durable.

questions.stem: A historian compares Victoria's 1855 tax on Chinese arrivals with the Pacific Solution of 2001. The strongest evidence of continuity between them is that both:
options: excluded people on explicitly racial grounds written into the text of the law
were opposed by all of the major political parties at the time they were introduced
were imposed on Australian governments by the British Colonial Office
responded to anxiety about unwanted arrivals by sea with measures meant to deter them
questions.explanation: Both policies aimed to discourage people from arriving by sea in response to public anxiety. The 2001 policy did not name any race, which marks an important change from the 1855 law.

questions.stem: Which judgement about continuity and change in race and belonging from 1834 to 2008 is best supported by evidence?
options: Racial exclusion was strongest after 1973 and weakest in the colonial period
Aboriginal people were treated as equal citizens from Federation onwards
Debates about immigration ended once multiculturalism became official policy
Race-based laws were largely dismantled, yet debates over who belongs kept recurring
questions.explanation: Laws that once excluded people by race were replaced by non-discriminatory immigration, the Racial Discrimination Act and the Apology, a profound change. Yet controversies from Blainey to Hanson and border security show that arguments about belonging continued.

questions.stem: Bringing Them Home traced the forcible removal of Aboriginal children back to protection laws such as Victoria's 1869 Act. This supports the argument that:
options: the removal of children ended at Federation, when the colonial protection boards were closed
child removal had roots in 19th-century protection laws and continued well into the 20th century
child removal began only with the assimilation policy agreed by ministers in 1961
19th-century protection laws had been designed to prevent the removal of children
questions.explanation: The inquiry found that removal policies operated from the colonial period until around 1970, under protection and then assimilation. Assimilation changed the justification but continued an older practice.
